title: Given a binary tree and a target sum, count all paths in the tree where the sum of the node values equals the target. The paths do not need to start at the root or end at a leaf, but they must go downward, from a node to one of its descendants. Explain the running-prefix-sum technique that makes this efficient.
shortTitle: Count Paths for a Sum (Count All Downward Paths Summing to a Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path, not only root-to-leaf paths, whose node values sum to a target. The efficient solution uses a running prefix sum from the root plus a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred along the current path. At each node, the number of valid paths ending at that node equals the count of the value `currentPrefix - target` already seen. The map is updated on the way down and rolled back on the way up, giving linear time and height-proportional space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a stream of charges flows down a chain of desks, and auditors want to count every contiguous downward stretch of charges that adds up to a flagged amount. A stretch can start at any desk, not just the top, and end at any lower desk. We walk down keeping a running total of charges, and we remember how often each running total has appeared; whenever running-total minus the flagged amount has appeared before, each earlier appearance marks the start of a matching stretch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a running prefix sum and a count map, and at each node add the number of earlier prefixes equal to current prefix minus the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path, not only root-to-leaf paths, whose node values sum to a target. The efficient solution uses a running prefix sum from the root plus a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred along the current path. At each node, the number of valid paths ending at that node equals the count of the value `currentPrefix - target` already seen. The map is updated on the way down and rolled back on the way up, giving linear time and height-proportional space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a stream of charges flows down a chain of desks, and auditors want to count every contiguous downward stretch of charges that adds up to a flagged amount. A stretch can start at any desk, not just the top, and end at any lower desk. We walk down keeping a running total of charges, and we remember how often each running total has appeared; whenever running-total minus the flagged amount has appeared before, each earlier appearance marks the start of a matching stretch.

**One line to remember:** Keep a running prefix sum and a count map, and at each node add the number of earlier prefixes equal to current prefix minus the target.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach tries every node as a path start and re-walks downward, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree. The prefix-sum technique removes the repeated work. We maintain `currentSum`, the sum from the root to the current node, and a map `prefixCounts` from a prefix-sum value to how many ancestors produced it. A downward path ending at the current node sums to the target exactly when some ancestor prefix equals `currentSum - target`, so we add `prefixCounts.getOrDefault(currentSum - target, 0)` to the answer.

We seed the map with `prefixCounts.put(0L, 1)` so a path that starts at the root itself is counted, because then `currentSum - target` is zero. Before recursing we increment the count for `currentSum`, and after recursing into both children we decrement it, for example `prefixCounts.merge(currentSum, -1, Integer::sum);`. This rollback keeps the map scoped to the current root-to-node path, so sibling branches never see each other's prefixes.

A senior-level nuance is the rollback: without it, a prefix from a left branch would wrongly count paths in a right branch that are not actually connected. Another nuance is using a `long` running sum to avoid overflow, and recognizing that negative node values are allowed, which is exactly why the prefix-sum trick is needed rather than early pruning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India logs charges down a desk chain, and fraud auditors want to count every contiguous downward run of charges that sums to a flagged suspicious amount. A suspicious run can begin at any desk in the middle of the chain, not only at the top, and can end at any desk below it. This is exactly how Count Paths for a Sum works: each downward run is a path, and we count all runs hitting the flagged amount.

Problem 2 — Recomputing every possible run from scratch would be far too slow on a deep desk chain. This is why we carry a running prefix sum and a map of how often each prefix appeared, so each node contributes its matching-run count in constant time, and we roll the map back as we climb so unrelated branches never interfere.

The code defines a `ChargeNode` holding a `BigDecimal` charge. A `CountPathsService` exposes `countFlaggedRuns(root, flagged)` returning an int. A `Demo` builds a charge tree with several matching downward runs and logs the count. Money is `BigDecimal`, and the prefix map keys on the scaled long-cents value to keep hashing exact.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: root 100, left -50 with child 150, right 50 with child 50; flagged amount 100 (10000 cents).

Step 1: Seed prefixCounts with {0: 1}. Enter root 100, currentSum 10000. needed = 10000 - 10000 = 0, and the map has one zero prefix, so one run is counted here, the single node 100. Record prefix 10000.

Step 2: Go left into -50, currentSum 10000 + (-5000) = 5000. needed = 5000 - 10000 = -5000, not present, zero runs. Record prefix 5000.

Step 3: Go into 150, currentSum 5000 + 15000 = 20000. needed = 20000 - 10000 = 10000, present once (from the root prefix), so one run counted, the downward run -50 then 150. Record and then roll back 20000, then 5000 on return.

Step 4: Go right into 50, currentSum 10000 + 5000 = 15000. needed = 15000 - 10000 = 5000, not present after rollback, zero. Record 15000. Go into 50, currentSum 15000 + 5000 = 20000. needed = 10000, present once (root), one run, the downward run 50 then 50. Roll back.

Step 5: Total runs = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.

FINE: At sum(cents)=20000 found 1 matching run(s)

sections.s6_takeaway:
Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path in a binary tree whose node values add up to a target, where a path may start and end at any node as long as it goes downward. The naive approach tries every node as a start and re-walks, which is quadratic on a skewed tree. I use the running-prefix-sum technique: I keep the sum from the root to the current node and a hash map of how many ancestors produced each prefix sum. At each node the number of valid paths ending there equals the number of earlier prefixes equal to the current sum minus the target, which I read from the map in constant time.

The two details I always call out are seeding and rollback. I seed the map with the value zero counted once so that a path starting right at the root is counted, and after visiting a node's children I decrement that node's prefix in the map so sibling branches never borrow each other's prefixes, which would otherwise count disconnected paths. I also carry the running sum as a long and allow negative node values, which is precisely why prefix sums are necessary instead of pruning.

At the National Bank of India I used this to scan charge chains for fraud, counting every contiguous downward run of desk charges that summed to a flagged amount, where a run could begin at any desk mid-chain. I stored charges as BigDecimal, converted them to exact long cents before hashing to avoid floating-point keys, seeded and rolled back the prefix map correctly, and reported the count to the fraud dashboard. Explaining why the prefix-sum map turns a quadratic scan into a linear one, and why the rollback keeps branches isolated, is what signals to an interviewer that I can optimise a tree traversal under real fraud-detection constraints.
